name: The Iron Law of Wages
statement: Real wages are dragged back toward bare subsistence, because higher pay only breeds more workers to compete it away.
statementAccent: higher pay only breeds more workers
meaning: The iron law of wages is a doctrine of classical political economy holding that real wages tend, in the long run, toward the minimum needed for a worker's subsistence. The mechanism is a population feedback loop: when wages rise above subsistence, workers can support more surviving children, so the labour supply grows and drives wages back down; when wages fall below subsistence, mortality rises, the labour supply shrinks, and wages are pushed back up. Subsistence therefore acts as a stable long-run resting point for wages. Grim in its implications and influential in nineteenth-century politics, the doctrine has since been decisively falsified by history.
mechanism: The engine is Malthus's population principle grafted onto Ricardo's distinction between the natural price of labour, the wage that lets workers subsist and just maintain their numbers, and the fluctuating market price. Any gap between the market wage and the subsistence wage is supposed to close automatically through demographic response: pay above subsistence raises the number of surviving workers and so the labour supply, dragging pay down, while pay below subsistence thins the workforce and lifts pay back up. Labour supply is thus made endogenous to the wage, chaining wages to subsistence and leaving no room for durable improvement in workers' real incomes.

examples.text: Ferdinand Lassalle deployed the iron law as a socialist argument that wages are locked at subsistence, so only abolishing the wage system itself could help workers, making it a centrepiece of early German social democracy.

David Ricardo's framework of a natural price of labour, toward which the market price gravitates, supplied the substance, though Ricardo himself allowed wages to stay above subsistence for long periods.
As industrial societies grew richer, birth rates fell rather than rose, breaking the population loop the doctrine assumed and letting real wages climb durably with productivity.

variants.name: Ricardo's nuance
variants.text: Ricardo held the market wage could stay above the subsistence natural wage for indefinitely long periods in an improving society, a far softer view than the rigid iron law later attributed to him.

variants.name: Marx's rejection
variants.text: In the Critique of the Gotha Programme, Karl Marx dismissed the iron law as Lassalle's and Malthus's, arguing that if it were a natural law, socialism could not abolish it, so basing socialist demands on it was self-defeating.

whyItMatters: The iron law of wages was one of the most consequential ideas of nineteenth-century economics and politics, giving a bleak, seemingly scientific reason to believe workers could never durably escape subsistence and lending force to socialist arguments against the wage system. Its later collapse is just as instructive: sustained productivity growth and the demographic transition, in which richer societies had fewer children, together shattered the population feedback the doctrine rested on, and real wages rose for generations.

working.text: recognise the doctrine's claim that any rise in wages is undone by a rise in the number of workers competing for them.
test the assumption that higher incomes raise birth rates, since the demographic transition shows the opposite and breaks the loop.

working.lead: Separate the name from the substance
working.text: credit Lassalle for the phrase but Ricardo and Malthus for the underlying ideas, and note Ricardo's own view was more nuanced.

limits: The doctrine is empirically failed. Real wages rose dramatically and durably in industrialising countries as productivity grew, contradicting any subsistence ceiling, and the demographic transition reversed the sign of its central assumption, since richer societies had fewer children, not more, severing the feedback loop it depends on. It also inherits the lump-of-labour error, treating more workers as only depressing wages while ignoring that population also raises labour demand. Even Ricardo, credited with the substance, held that wages could remain above subsistence for indefinitely long periods, so the rigid iron form overstates the classical economists it claimed as authority.
misreadings: The phrase and its rigid form should not be attributed to Ricardo or Malthus; Lassalle coined the name in 1862, while Ricardo, who supplied the natural-price framework, did not use iron law and expressly allowed wages to stay above subsistence for long periods. Marx did not endorse the doctrine; he explicitly ridiculed it as Lassallean and Malthusian. The population mechanism is not that higher wages raise birth rates in the modern world, since the demographic transition shows the reverse. And subsistence was not always a fixed biological floor, as classical writers sometimes allowed a socially determined minimum.
origin: The phrase 'iron law of wages', in German 'ehernes Lohngesetz', was coined by Ferdinand Lassalle in 1862, drawing on David Ricardo's natural price of labour and Thomas Malthus's population theory; the doctrine was later rejected by Karl Marx and refuted by the demographic transition.
